messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Katherine was twenty-three the first time she was trapped. A house fire in a row of attached brick rowhomes—electrical, they said later, starting in the basement and climbing through the walls before anyone saw smoke. She had been on the nozzle, following the line in ahead of her lieutenant, when the floor gave way. Not a collapse you could call dramatic—just a rotten joist that let go beneath her left boot, dropping her into the basement below with debris pinning her pelvis and both legs. For forty-seven minutes she lay under a section of flooring, her faceplate fogging, the air in her tank ticking down, while the fire crackled somewhere above and the rest of the crew worked to extricate her. She remembered later the exact pattern of char on the beam three inches from her right eye, and the sound of a dripping pipe that matched her own heart rate. She had been certain, for the first twenty minutes, that she was going to die—not because she was injured but because no one seemed to be coming fast enough, and the darkness felt alive and pressing in on her from all sides. When they finally pulled her out, she was hyperventilating into her mask and her hands would not stop shaking. She told the chief she was fine. She drove herself to the ER. No broken bones, just bruising and a deep, unnameable dread that she could not shake.

In the months that followed, that dread crystallised into something more specific. Ordinary sounds began to startle her: the hiss of an air brake on the engine, a dropped tool in the station bay, the clatter of a metal chair scraping concrete. She would jump, and then feel foolish, and then feel a spike of fear that had no obvious reason. Crowded spaces—the station kitchen during shift change, the grocery store on a Saturday—made her chest tighten until she had to find an exit. At first she attributed it to lingering anxiety from the accident. But the memories did not fade in the usual way. When she closed her eyes, she saw the charred beam as clearly as if it were still inches from her face, more vivid and immediate than any ordinary recollection. She began to keep her phone camera roll scrupulously cleared, because an old photo—of the station, of herself before the accident, even of something completely unrelated like a birthday party—could trigger a sudden, full-sense replay: the weight of the debris, the smell of damp ash, the drip-drip-drip of that pipe. The memories felt like they belonged to someone else, a stranger who had been buried alive in a basement, not to Katherine, the firefighter who had always been the calm one on the crew. She started to wonder if she even knew who that calm person was anymore.

Her self-blame was relentless. She replayed every choice she had made that night: she had stepped to the left, she had not checked the floor with her tool, she had advanced too quickly. The event happened because of the way I acted, she told herself, and that conclusion spilled over into everything. A minor irritation at work—a misplaced hose, a delayed radio check—sent her into a spiral of self-criticism. I can’t deal with even the slightest upset, she thought, and the thought became a conviction. She stopped volunteering for overtime. She avoided the captain’s office. She laughed less, talked less, and began to feel like a ghost in her own body. Her colleagues noticed; they asked if she was okay. She said she was fine.

What finally brought Katherine to seek help was an episode she could not explain away. She had been at the station, sitting in the common room, when the television cut to a documentary clip of a fire scene. For a split second—she was not even sure what triggered it—she was back under the debris, the weight crushing her chest, the darkness absolute. She rose out of her chair, knocked over a coffee mug, and stood in the middle of the room with her hands out, trembling, before she realised she was in a safe place. She could not relax afterward, even alone in her bunk that night, her eyes fixed on the ceiling, her body waiting for something to collapse. She made an appointment the next morning. She is most afraid that this version of herself—the one who can no longer trust her own judgment, who flinches at a dropped pan, who does not recognise the woman in old photographs—is the only version she will ever be again. She is hoping, more than she can say, to be wrong.
